answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — an anonymous advertising slogan
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Einstein ever said or wrote this. Quote Investigator traces the “eighth wonder of the world” & compound-interest pairing to an April 1925 bank advertisement in the Cleveland Plain Dealer, printed with no attribution; the Einstein credit does not appear until 1988. The extra clause — “He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it” — is a still-later embellishment with no documented source.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Cleveland Plain Dealer bank ad, 27 Apr 1925

source.excerpt: “Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn’t, pays it.”
trail: Quote Investigator dates the “eighth wonder”/compound-interest pairing to a 27 April 1925 advertisement for The Equity Savings & Loan Company in the Cleveland Plain Dealer — printed with no attribution.

Over the years the line was reassigned to impressive names: Baron Rothschild (a 1965 Wall Street Journal ad), John D. Rockefeller (a 1981 newspaper column), and finally Albert Einstein (a 1988 financial-analyst attribution), per QI’s research.
Princeton University Press’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein places the saying in its “Probably Not By Einstein” section — no credible source connects it to him.
source.excerptNote: The one-line “eighth wonder” core is documented from 1925; the “He who understands it…” extension is a later, unsourced addition.

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identifiable author. The one-line core surfaces in anonymous 1925 advertising copy, and the popular full quotation with “He who understands it, earns it…” has no documented origin at all — so no copyright status can honestly be asserted.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) developed the theory of relativity and won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. Because his name is shorthand for genius, he has become the internet’s single greatest magnet for invented quotations — finance, self-help & motivational lines are routinely pinned on him to borrow his authority. Princeton University Press files this compound-interest saying under “Probably Not By Einstein.”

copyAttribution: Misattributed to Albert Einstein. No evidence he said it; the "eighth wonder / compound interest" line traces to an unattributed 1925 bank advertisement (Cleveland Plain Dealer). Source: Quote Investigator.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: The saying is a classic “celebrity upgrade” — anonymous marketing copy that acquired a famous author to sound authoritative. It has been pinned on at least three different luminaries.

items.why: The earliest Einstein credit QI could find dates to 1988 — 33 years after his death — and Princeton’s The Ultimate Quotable Einstein files it under “Probably Not By Einstein.”
The same line was credited to Rothschild in a 1965 Wall Street Journal ad and to Rockefeller in a 1981 newspaper column — neither with any real source.

items.scope: The “He who understands it, earns it” extension
items.why: This motivational tail is a modern embellishment; it does not appear in the 1925 source and has no documented origin of its own.

misattribution.truthLine: The phrase began as an unattributed 1925 bank advertisement and was later dressed up with famous names; no evidence ties it to Einstein.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The underlying idea — that compounding is astonishingly powerful over time — is sound, which is exactly why the line spreads. But its rhetorical punch comes from the Einstein byline, not from anything Einstein wrote. Financial marketers have leaned on the “eighth wonder” framing since the 1920s precisely because it makes an ordinary savings pitch feel like received wisdom.
context.pull: Anonymous ad copy from 1925, upgraded to “Einstein” by 1988.
